label: Regional news sites, DE/AT (Xu et al. 2025)
definition: Non-subscribing devices that clicked a 'subscribe now' button on a paywalled article, divided by non-subscribing devices that hit the paywall.
population: 3,518,822 devices that hit the paywall across 21 regional/local news sites (20 German, 1 Austrian), two one-week windows (5-11 May and 5-11 Aug 2022)
source_title: Converting Online News Visitors to Subscribers: Exploring the Effectiveness of Paywall Strategies Using Behavioural Data (Journalism Studies)
quote: Regarding whether the 'subscribe now' button was clicked, 3,518,822 individual-level cases were included, and regarding whether a subscription was taken out the number was 28,506.
notes: Rate computed from the two counts the paper reports (28,506 / 3,518,822). The paper does not report what share of the 28,506 clickers completed payment.

label: Showing a deck or intro paragraph on the paywalled article
definition: Odds ratio for clicking the 'subscribe now' button when the paywalled article shows a stand-first/deck (OR 0.137) or an introductory paragraph (OR 0.278), other variables held constant.
population: Same sample as above; 42 website-period cases weighted by 3,518,822 devices
source_title: Xu et al. 2025, Journalism Studies
quote: displaying a stand-first ('deck' in US-English) on the paywall locked article page significantly decreases the odds of visitors clicking the 'subscribe now' button, by 86.3%. ... displaying an intro also significantly decreases the odds of clicking the button: by 72.2%.
notes: Directly relevant to the 'read the beginning, then pay' design: the more of the article the teaser gives away, the fewer readers start the subscription flow. Discounts raised the odds of completing payment 3.35x (p = .034).

label: Tightening the NYT paywall (fewer free articles, gated sections)
definition: Difference-in-differences estimates of a 2013-era NYT policy change on article consumption and on new subscriptions; 12,023 of 38,490 new subscriptions over the study attributed to the change.
population: Panel of 29,705,796 users over 212 days
source_title: Digital Paywall Design: Implications for Content Demand and Subscriptions (Management Science)
quote: The paywall policy changes we studied suppressed total content demand by about 9.9%, reducing total advertising revenue. However, this decrease was more than offset by increased subscription revenue as the policy change led to a 31% increase in total subscriptions during our seven-month study, yielding net positive revenues of over $230,000.
notes: Among users who actually hit the paywall, consumption fell 18.7% to 19.2%. The paper does not report a hit-to-subscribe conversion rate.

label: Launching the NYT paywall (March 2011)
definition: Difference-in-differences estimate of the paywall's effect on unique visitors versus comparable newspapers without a paywall.
population: Individual-level NYT panel data, Jan 2010 to Dec 2013
source_title: Paywalls: Monetizing Online Content (Journal of Marketing)
quote: Our results reveal that the number of unique visitors decreased by 16.8% as a result of the paywall ... the paywall adversely impacted the number of unique visitors by 11.3% among light users and 57.2% among heavy users.
notes: Print subscriptions rose 1 to 4% versus the counterfactual (spillover). The paper computes roughly $97.5 million of online subscription revenue for the NYT in 2013.

label: Introducing a paywall at local news sites (field test)
definition: Change in visits after a media publisher's field test introduced paywalls across several local media markets.
population: Several local media markets, one US publisher
source_title: Paywalls and the demand for news (Information Economics and Policy)
quote: We find a 51% drop in visits after the introduction of a paywall and a far larger drop for younger readers.
notes: Abstract-level figure; the underlying paywall was a hard paywall on local news, the harshest case.

label: Freemium products generally (software, games, web services)
definition: Share of a freemium product's users who are premium (paying) subscribers, as characterised in the literature review of this paper.
population: Literature statement, not a measured dataset
source_title: The effect of free sampling strategies on freemium conversion rates (Electronic Markets)
quote: Despite the many benefits of freemium, most firms suffer from too few premium subscribers (3-5 %), which challenges their profitability.
notes: Included as a cross-industry anchor only. Value plotted at the midpoint of the stated range.

label: Most-viewed post, one Substack writer (Lori Ballen)
definition: Paid subscriptions Substack attributed to the post, divided by the post's total views (Substack counts repeat views).
population: One writer, six months (Jan to Jul 2026), 202 paid subscribers gained in total
source_title: My Most-Viewed Substack Post Got 8,100 Views and 2 Paid Subscribers. Here's What Actually Converts.
quote: My most-viewed post of the entire six months pulled just over 8,100 views. ... It made exactly two paid subscribers.
notes: The page does not say whether this post was paywalled. The ten-post table with per-post numbers sits behind a teaser paywall and could not be read.

label: Best-converting post, same writer (Lori Ballen)
definition: Same metric; the denominator is an upper bound because the page says the post had 'less than half the traffic' of the 8,100-view post.
population: One writer, same six months
source_title: Lori Ballen, July 2026
quote: Then I looked at the post that actually converted the most readers into paying subscribers. It got less than half the traffic. And it brought in fifteen. ... one of them converted at more than seven times the rate of a post that reached twice as many people.
notes: A 15x spread between posts by the same writer in the same period: post topic dominates any platform average.

label: Paid sign-ups per click on a Substack Note, 194 creators
definition: Paid subscriptions Substack attributed to a Note, divided by clicks on that Note (a click lands on the publication or a post, not necessarily a paywalled one).
population: 194 creators with 1,000+ Note clicks in both H1 2025 and H1 2026; dataset of 711,199 Notes
source_title: Your Notes Convert Half as Well as They Did Last Year (The Writing Edge)
quote: Paid conversion for the same creators did not move: 0.021 per hundred clicks then, 0.019 now. ... a click on a Note produced 1.74 free subscribers per hundred in the first half of 2025 and 0.93 in the first half of 2026
notes: Third-party dataset; Substack does not publish how it attributes a subscription to a Note. Free sign-ups per click are roughly 50 to 90x the paid rate.

label: People shown Substack's free-month offer who end up paying
value_text: 5% take the trial; over 50% then renew (about 2.5% pay)
definition: Share of people who see a writer's free-month offer who accept it, times the share who renew as paying subscribers after the month. The 2.5% is the product of the two stated figures.
population: Platform-wide, no sample or method given
source_title: How Substack Enables The Growth Engine For Your Newsletter (On Substack, Dec 28 2022)
quote: About 5% of people who see the free-month offer take it. Over 50% go on to renew their paid subscription after the free month.
notes: The closest official Substack figure to an offer-impression conversion rate. It is an upgrade offer, not a mid-post paywall, so treat it as an upper-bound analogue.

label: beehiiv, median publication with paid turned on
definition: Median paid conversion rate across beehiiv publications with paid subscriptions enabled. The report never defines the denominator; its own gloss ('for every 1,000 subscribers, about 6 are paying') implies total subscribers.
population: 'Thousands of publications on beehiiv', first-party data, 2021 to 2026
source_title: The State of Paid Newsletters 2026 (beehiiv)
quote: The median paid conversion rate across beehiiv is 0.62%. ... For every 1,000 subscribers, about 6 are paying.
notes: Only publications that switched paid on. Industry medians: Sports 1.93%, Investing 0.84%, Finance 0.78%. Median price $10/month, $100/year. Median monthly churn 5.06% (Food & Drink) to 16.67% (Money).

label: beehiiv, top 10% of publications, by industry
definition: 90th-percentile paid conversion rate within each industry; same undefined denominator as the median.
population: Same report
source_title: The State of Paid Newsletters 2026 (beehiiv)
quote: Top-decile conversion ranges from 5.55% (Technology) to 30.80% (Economy), with Finance and Investing at 20.00% and 18.69%.
notes: A 10x to 50x gap between the median and the top decile: the distribution is extremely skewed.

label: Substack's own guidance
definition: Share of free subscribers who convert to paid, as stated in Substack's going-paid guide. No date, sample or method.
population: Unstated ('we tend to see')
source_title: Substack: Going paid guide
quote: We tend to see 5-10% of free subscribers convert to paying subscriptions, with 10% being a rate to aim for.
notes: Every secondary '5 to 10%' claim traces back to this one sentence. Independent data below sits well under it.

label: Substack publications, self-reported (Campbell dataset)
definition: Median of self-reported paid conversion rates gathered from Notes, articles and Reddit posts. Denominator (free vs total subscribers) not stated.
population: 'Hundreds of reports' over five years, publications from under 100 to tens of thousands of subscribers
source_title: What Is The Average Paid Subscriber Conversion Rate on Substack? (Really Good Business Ideas)
quote: the median paid subscriber conversion rate is 3% ... only 20% of publications have a conversion rate higher than 5% ... I have only seen two reports of a 10% paid subscriber conversion rate; both were from small publications
notes: Self-selected: writers who publish their numbers skew toward the successful. The most-cited independent Substack figure.

label: Substack platform-wide pooled ratio (paid / active subscriptions)
value_text: about 10 to 14% (5M paid of 35M to 50M active)
definition: Total paid subscriptions divided by total active subscriptions, both as reported by Substack. Counts subscriptions, not people, and is dominated by the largest publications.
population: Platform totals: 5M paid (Mar 2025); 35M active (Mar 2025, Tubefilter citing Substack) or 50M active (Apr 2026, citing Substack's About page)
source_title: 5 million (The Substack Post, Mar 11 2025)
quote: Today we are celebrating 5 million paid subscriptions on Substack.
notes: A pooled ratio, not a median: it says nothing about the typical publication. The active-subscription base differs by source (35M vs 50M), hence the range.

label: Platformer after year one (Casey Newton)
definition: Share of free subscribers who went paid in the first year.
population: One large publication
source_title: What I learned from a year on Substack (Platformer)
quote: Guidance I had gotten from Substack suggested I might expect 10 percent or so of my free subscribers to go paid. Instead, it was closer to 5 percent. That number has grown a bit over the past year, but it's still well under 10.
notes: Also: 'Platformer loses 3-4 percent of its paid customers per month.'

label: Lenny's Newsletter (via Growth In Reverse)
definition: Paid subscribers divided by all subscribers.
population: One very large publication
source_title: Growth In Reverse: Lenny's paid newsletter (Dec 3 2024)
quote: He has over 377k free subscribers, and over 18,000 paid subscribers ... he is able to get between 4-5% of all subscribers to pay for a subscription
notes: Survivorship: the publications whose numbers get written up are the successes.

label: Tangle at paid launch (Isaac Saul, via Poynter)
definition: Share of existing subscribers who paid when a paid Friday edition launched.
population: One publication, launch moment
source_title: How much does Substack pay reporters? (Poynter, Apr 23 2026)
quote: When he launched a paid Friday newsletter, 15% of his subscribers converted.
notes: Same article: The Handbasket has 'roughly 31,000 total subscribers, including around 4,100 paid' (about 13%, computed) at $8/month.

label: The Product Compass, paywalls 3 of 4 posts (via Karen Cherry)
definition: Paid divided by free subscribers for a publication that locks three posts a month and leaves about 1,000 words free above each paywall.
population: One publication, public stats as described by a third party
source_title: $156,960 Per Year From Substack: Steal This Strategy (Karen Cherry, Apr 2025)
quote: 1,962 paying subscribers and $156,960 per year in estimated revenue ... 92K+ free ... conversion rate for The Product Compass is 2% ... three locked posts and one unlocked post each month
notes: Reported by the agent from fetched text fragments; the page presents these as separate figures rather than one sentence.

label: Small publication after 14 months of paywalling (Ryan Turner)
definition: Paid divided by email subscribers after 14 months with paywalls in place.
population: One small publication
source_title: Paywalls removed, paid subscriptions off (Ryan Turner, Jun 2026)
quote: 472 email subscribers ... exactly two paid subscribers ... 0.4%
notes: Reported by the agent from fetched text fragments. A counter-example to the survivorship in the rows above: the writer switched paid off.

label: Moving the paywall later in the post (Andi Bitay)
value_text: 0 vs 4, then 2 vs 6 paid sign-ups in the first hour
definition: New paid subscribers in the hour after publishing, comparing a paywall placed near the top with one placed where the solution or first step begins.
population: One writer, two posts; no views or list size given
source_title: How to Place Your Paywall So Readers Actually Subscribe (Nov 2025)
quote: I put the paywall near the beginning without much strategy. Just a separation point. Result after one hour: 0 new paid subscribers. ... I moved the paywall to where the solution was about to begin ... Result after one hour: 4 new paid subscribers.
notes: Sequential edits, not a randomised test. Direction agrees with the peer-reviewed finding above that the teaser content changes behaviour, though there the richer teaser reduced subscribe clicks.

label: Publications that paywall some content vs all-free (Substack claim)
definition: Average revenue of publications that paywall at least some content versus publications that publish everything free.
population: No sample or method given
source_title: How do paid subscriptions on Substack work? (Substack FAQ, Nov 2022)
quote: publications that paywall at least some of their content make on average five times as much revenue as publications that publish all their content for free!
notes: Obvious selection effect: publications that paywall are the ones that turned paid on at all. Not evidence that paywalling a given post raises revenue.

label: Where new paid subscribers come from (Diana Dovgopol)
value_text: 58% of new paid subs were existing free readers
definition: Share of one writer's 2026 paid sign-ups who were already on the free list before upgrading; she paywalls 27% of posts (17 of 64).
population: One writer's dashboard plus five tracked publications
source_title: How to Grow on Substack (Sep 16 2026)
quote: In 2026 I added hundreds of paid subscribers. 58%, were people already sitting on my free list who upgraded. They didn't arrive from a note. They had been reading me free for weeks, and then one article moved them.
notes: Supports the pattern that paywalled posts mostly convert warm readers, not new traffic.

label: How many newsletters paywall at all (InboxReads directory, 2025)
value_text: 2% fully paid, 8% free with a paid upgrade, 91% free
definition: Share of newsletters submitted to the InboxReads directory in 2025 by monetisation type; 'paid upgrades' fell from 12% the year before.
population: Directory submissions (count not stated), cross-platform, self-selected
source_title: State of Newsletters 2025 (InboxReads, Dec 2025)
quote: The percentage of paid newsletters submitted in 2025 was just 2%, the same as last year. Newsletters with paid upgrades dropped from 12% of submissions ot 8%. Free newsletters grew from 87% to 91%.
notes: The only multi-platform figure found for how common paywalling is.

label: 500+ publishers, median (Lenfest / Press+ data, 2011-2018)
definition: Paid stop conversion rate (PSCR): readers who subscribe in a month as a share of all users stopped by the meter or paywall that month. Percentiles: 10th 0.24%, 50th 0.54%, 80th 1.04%, 90th 1.31%, 95th 1.93%.
population: More than 500 news organisations with subscription or membership models, 2011 to 2018, mostly US newspapers on the Press+ system; desktop-heavy
source_title: Digital Subscription Reader Revenue Benchmarks & Best Practices from 500+ Publications Worldwide (Lenfest Institute, Matt Skibinski, 2019), slide 28
quote: Once users are stopped by a meter message, conversion becomes the focus ... Percentile PSCR 95% 1.93% 90% 1.31% 80% 1.04% 70% 0.83% 60% 0.62% 50% 0.54% 40% 0.47% 30% 0.40% 20% 0.33% 10% 0.24% 5% 0.21%
notes: The single best source for this metric: a defined denominator, a percentile table and a large sample. Its weakness is age (much of the data is 2011 to 2016).

label: 500+ publishers, top decile (same dataset)
definition: Same metric, upper percentiles. The companion Shorenstein playbook rounds this to 'the top decile ... 1.3 percent of stopped unique visitors per month' against 'the median ... 0.5 percent'.
population: Same as above
source_title: Digital Pay-Meter Playbook (Shorenstein Center and Lenfest Institute, Aug 2019)
quote: while the top decile of publishers studied generally converted an average of 1.3 percent of stopped unique visitors per month, the median 50 percent of publishers only converted 0.5 percent of unique visitors.
notes: Even the best publishers convert only about 1 to 2 in 100 stopped readers per month.

label: 103 US local news markets, median (Mather Economics, Q2 2022)
definition: 'Paywall Conversion Rate', reported next to 'Paywall Hit Rate' (median 14.3%) and 'Conversions per 1M users' (median 513). The PDF never defines the denominator; the framing implies conversions divided by users who hit the paywall.
population: 103 markets (100 US, 3 international), 387 million unique visitors, April to June 2022, quarterly medians
source_title: Listener Digital Audience Benchmarking Report, September 2022 (Mather Economics)
quote: Paywall Hit Rate Median 14.3% Best-in-Class 20.3% Paywall Conversion Rate Median 0.22% Best-in-Class 0.58% Conversions per 1M Users Median 513 / million Best-in-Class 1,263 / million
notes: Earlier editions: 0.25% (Q1 2021, best 0.46%) and 0.21% (Q1 2022, best 0.60%). Mather noted that as more users hit the wall, 'the Paywall Conversion Rate remains stable'.

label: One major US newspaper, immediate subscriptions (Kanuri, Overby & Pattabhiramaiah, 2026)
definition: Share of paywall encounters that end in an immediate subscription, from one year of clickstream data at a major US newspaper.
population: 209.2 million page views, one newspaper, one year
source_title: Please Subscribe to Continue Reading: An Empirical Analysis of Readers' Responses to Newspaper Paywalls (forthcoming, MIS Quarterly; Notre Dame release, Jun 16 2026)
quote: 59.2 percent of readers leave the site immediately after reaching a paywall ... Only about two out of every 1,000 readers subscribe on the spot ... those who encountered it were 84 times more likely to subscribe
notes: INMA's write-up of the same research programme gives 0.21% of stops and says this is 'in line with' its own 300+-brand benchmark, whose figure is members-only.

label: Local Media Association benchmarking goal (via WebPublisherPro)
definition: Paid stop conversion rate a publisher should aim for, attributed to Local Media Association benchmarking data.
population: Not stated; the LMA primary was not located
source_title: How does your conversion rate compare to other publishers? (WebPublisherPro)
quote: publishers who are tracking their Paid Stop Conversion Rate (PSCR) should be looking at .5% as a goal. ... If you have ever wondered what percentage of people actually subscribed after hitting a paywall on your website, this is how you'll find your answer.
notes: Secondary source; consistent with the Lenfest median.

label: Pelcro vendor blog (unsourced claim)
definition: 'Industry benchmarks' for metered paywall conversion among readers who hit the paywall, with no sample, period or source.
population: None stated
source_title: Conversion Rate Best Practices for Publishers (Pelcro, May 2026)
quote: Industry benchmarks for metered paywall conversion typically range from 1% to 5% of readers who hit the paywall
notes: Included so the outlier is visible: 2 to 10x every measured figure above. Treat as marketing.

label: Paywall click-through, market average (Poool / The Audiencers)
value_text: 0.2% click the paywall's button; 3% is the target
definition: Users who click the call-to-action on the paywall, divided by users who see the paywall. Poool explicitly declines to give a paywall-to-paid benchmark for the final step.
population: Poool client base and a study of 75 (French) publishers; period not stated
source_title: Increase subscription conversion rates by 46% through optimizing each of these smaller steps by just 10% (The Audiencers)
quote: The market average is 0.2%, but our clients see a lot higher when following our optimization recommendations, so the target percentage of users to convert here is 3%. ... The average conversion rate here varies hugely from publisher to publisher ... we can't really pull out a benchmark that is of any value.
notes: Lower than the 0.81% computed from Xu et al.; both say that under 1 in 100 stopped readers even starts the checkout.

label: Checkout completion after clicking (10 US metro dailies)
value_text: 9.9% of desktop users who reach the offer page complete payment (5.3% mobile)
definition: Confirmation-page reaches as a share of users who saw the first step of the purchase funnel (offer and pricing page). Not a paywall-hit rate: it is the step after the click.
population: 10 major metropolitan newspapers
source_title: Digital Pay-Meter Playbook (Shorenstein Center and Lenfest Institute, Aug 2019)
quote: only 29 percent of desktop users who saw the first step of the purchase funnel (presentation of offers and pricing choices) made it to the second step (providing their email address). Only 14.8 percent reached the step of the process at which they were asked to enter payment information, and 9.9 percent reached the confirmation page
notes: Chain check: 0.2 to 0.8% click, times 5 to 10% complete, gives 0.01 to 0.08% immediate conversions per stop, below the monthly PSCR medians because PSCR also counts later and indirect subscriptions.

label: Anonymous visitors vs known users (Piano, 550+ publishers)
definition: Subscription conversion rate of anonymous visitors versus users already known (registered or logged in). Period not stated.
population: More than 550 enterprise clients, 140 billion pageviews a month
source_title: Subscription Performance Benchmark Report 2022 (Piano)
quote: While the conversion rate for anonymous visitors is just 0.22%, conversion rises to 9.88% for known users. That's a dramatic 45X difference. ... On average, approximately 3% of registered users convert to a paid subscription within a year of registration.
notes: Relevant to newsletters: a reader who hits a paywall inside an email they subscribed to is a known user, not an anonymous visitor. Piano's Q4 2019 medians by referrer: email 0.62%, direct 0.24%, Google 0.16%, Facebook 0.06%.

label: Conversions per unique user, US local news (Mather, Q2 2022)
definition: Monthly subscription conversions divided by monthly unique users, all traffic.
population: 103 markets, 387 million unique visitors, April to June 2022
source_title: Listener Digital Audience Benchmarking Report, September 2022 (Mather Economics)
quote: Conversions per 1M Users Median 513 / million Best-in-Class 1,263 / million
notes: Percentages computed from the per-million figures. Roughly: 14% of users hit the wall, 0.22% of those convert, giving about 0.03 to 0.05% of all users.

label: Subscribers as a share of monthly visitors, 166 publishers (INMA via Press Gazette)
definition: Total digital subscribers divided by monthly unique visitors: a stock-to-traffic ratio, not a per-visit conversion.
population: 166 publishers in 33 countries, end of 2022
source_title: Newsbrand subscriber conversion: which brands have the best rate (Press Gazette)
quote: According to an International News Media Association (INMA) study of 166 publishers in 33 countries at the end of last year, the median was 0.6%, while the 25% of brands who performed best had a rate of at least 1.4%.
notes: Press Gazette's own Similarweb-based ratios for big brands: The Athletic 16%, WSJ 10 to 15%, Nikkei 0.2%.

label: Tightening the paywall at 91 sites vs loosening at 27 (Mather, 2023-24)
value_text: Hits more than doubled; conversion rate per hit -20%; sign-ups +46%
definition: One-year outcomes after 118 US news sites changed paywall strategy in March 2023.
population: 118 websites, 91 tightened, 27 loosened
source_title: Paywall Intercept Rates on 'Closed' and 'Open' News Sites Yield Revenue Optimization Insights (Mather Economics, Jun 2024)
quote: The tighter paywall group had a greater increase in conversions per million users than the open paywall group because the number of sales attempts (+100%) outweighed the reduction in conversion rate (-20%). ... Websites employing a stricter paywall strategy observed a 46% increase in average sign-ups.
notes: Same direction as the NYT quasi-experiment: more stops beat a lower per-stop rate. 'The Closed group saw larger declines in users and page views.'

label: What readers do when they hit a paywall (one major US newspaper)
value_text: 59% leave at once; 18% read free content; 13% look for unwalled articles; 10% bypass
definition: Distribution of immediate responses to a paywall encounter.
population: 209.2 million page views, one year
source_title: Kanuri, Overby & Pattabhiramaiah (Notre Dame release, Jun 2026)
quote: 59.2 percent of readers leave the site immediately after reaching a paywall ... Approximately 18 percent shift to free content elsewhere on the site, about 13 percent click around in search of articles that are not behind the paywall and about one in 10 successfully bypasses the paywall
notes: Six in ten readers who hit the wall are gone immediately; the wall still makes them 84 times more likely to subscribe than readers who never hit it.

label: Share of monthly users stopped, by wall type (INMA, 318 brands, Q2 2026)
value_text: Hard walls stop 56%+ of users; freemium or hybrid walls 25% or fewer
definition: Users stopped by the wall as a share of monthly users, by paywall model. Freemium/hybrid sites had 67% higher reach.
population: 318 news brands benchmarking with INMA, Q2 2026
source_title: How long is the shadow of The New York Times' paywall? (INMA, Sep 2026)
quote: In Q2 2026, most news Web sites with hard walls were stopping at least 56% of users monthly, while most sites with freemium or hybrid walls — 25% or fewer users. The freemium or hybrid-walled sites enjoyed 67% higher online reach
notes: A Substack-style partial paywall is a freemium wall. Older data: Lenfest median stop rate 1.8% (2011-18), 'sustainable' publishers at 4.2%+; Mather medians 8 to 14% (2021-22).

label: Conversion by wall type, relative (Piano, 2021)
value_text: Hard wall 10x soft wall; soft wall 2x bottom ribbon; landing page 25x hard wall
definition: Relative conversion per impression by offer type; Piano publishes no absolute rates by type.
population: 'Hundreds of organizations, thousands of websites and billions of visitors'
source_title: Subscription Performance Benchmarks, Spring 2021 (Piano)
quote: Hard paywalls have 10 times higher conversion rates than soft paywalls, which have double the conversion rate of bottom ribbons. Landing pages have 25 times higher conversion rates than hard paywalls.
notes: Higher conversion per impression on hard walls comes with far more readers lost (see the stop-rate row).

label: What triggered subscribers to pay (API survey of 4,100 new subscribers)
value_text: 50% say hitting the meter triggered them; 45% a promotion or free trial
definition: Self-reported triggers among recent digital subscribers to 90 US local newspapers, Nov to Dec 2017.
population: 4,100+ recent subscribers, converters only
source_title: Paths to Subscription (American Press Institute / Media Insight Project, Feb 2018)
quote: 50% of digital subscribers are triggered to subscribe by hitting a paywall meter ... 45% finally subscribed because of a promotion or a free trial
notes: Says nothing about non-converters, but confirms the wall is the single most common trigger among those who do pay.
